Thonon
to-non'
n. (chief town of the Chablais on Lake Geneva; Reformed under Bern from 1536 and recovered for Rome by the mission of 1594)
French Thonon, from a pre-Latin root, perhaps Celtic dunum, a fort; the town stands on the south shore of Lake Geneva below the Savoy hills.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Thonon is the chief town of the Chablais, the Savoyard country on the southern shore of Lake Geneva, and it changed its religion twice in sixty years. When Bern overran Savoy in 1536 the Chablais was taken with the Vaud and reformed by mandate; for a generation it had Reformed ministers, and its religious houses were suppressed. In 1564 the treaty of Lausanne returned the Chablais to Savoy, and the duke, unable at first to undo the settlement, left it alone. Then in 1594 the bishop of Geneva, resident at Annecy, sent Francis de Sales and a small mission into the Chablais, with the duke's protection and later his soldiers. Over four years they preached, disputed, printed broadsheets against the Reformed ministers, visited, and held public processions; by 1598 the Chablais was substantially Catholic again, and the Reformed ministry was gone. The dictionary enters Thonon because it is the one episode in this batch in which the Reformed were out-preached. The mission used the methods the Reformation itself had used—vernacular preaching, printed argument, catechising, personal visitation, patience—and the Reformed church of the Chablais, planted by a conqueror's mandate and never rooted in the people, could not answer them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a mission as a body of persons sent to propagate religion; a broadside as a sheet printed on one side; and to recover as to regain possession of a thing lost.

expand to see more

MISSION, n. A sending or being sent; persons sent to propagate religion; a station of missionaries.

BROADSIDE, n. A sheet of paper containing matter printed on one side only, and intended for general circulation.

RECOVER, v.t. [L. recupero.] To regain; to get or obtain that which was lost; to restore from sickness or depression.

PROCESSION, n. [L. processio.] A train of persons walking or riding in ceremonious solemnity, as in a religious observance.

ROOTED, adj. Fixed; deep; firmly implanted; radical.

Key Scripture

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

2Ti 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Act 17:11 — "These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so."

Mat 7:15 — "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves."

Modern Corruption

Chablais town reformed by Bernese mandate in 1536 and recovered for Rome between 1594 and 1598 by a mission that preached, printed and visited.

expand to see more

The doctrines the Chablais mission restored are the doctrines the Reformation called the church away from, and the dictionary names them: the Mass as a sacrifice, the invocation of saints, the authority of the papal see, the veneration of images, and the whole system of merit. That the mission conducted itself largely by argument rather than by the sword does not make its doctrine true, and the duke's soldiers were in the country throughout.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the episode teaches against the Reformed. A church established by mandate and maintained by a foreign magistrate had, after fifty years, no body of catechised and persuaded people to stand on, and it fell to a mission of a few men with a press and a willingness to walk. “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) is the ministry's work, and the Chablais ministers had not done it in a form the people could use. The dictionary takes this as the standing refutation of the territorial method: what a decree establishes, a preacher can take away.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek antilego (G483), to gainsay; Greek anakrino (G350), to examine or sift.

expand to see more

Greek antechomai (G472) — to hold fast to; “Holding fast the faithful word”, Titus 1:9.

Greek antilego (G483) — to speak against, to gainsay; “to convince the gainsayers”, Titus 1:9.

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; “Preach the word”, 2 Timothy 4:2.

Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift; “searched the scriptures daily”, Acts 17:11.

Greek pseudoprophetes (G5578) — a false prophet; “Beware of false prophets”, Matthew 7:15.

Usage

"“by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — the work the Chablais ministers had not done."

"“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — the method the mission of 1594 used, and used well."

"“searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — what a decreed establishment had never taught its people to do."
